name: wasm-perf (Emscripten Wasm SIMD intrinsics vs JavaScript matrix multiply)
workload: Time to complete 10,000 multiplications of two 64 x 64 matrices, JavaScript vs C compiled to WebAssembly by Emscripten with and without -O3 and -msimd128 and with SIMD intrinsics, plus native GCC rows.
claimed_speedup: mul_mats_intrin-wasm-simd-O3.js 0.245s vs JavaScript 5.768s (-95.8%, about 23.5x faster, derived from page data); -O3 -msimd128 auto-vectorised 0.278s (-95.2%); -O3 without SIMD 2.012s (-65%); wasm built without -O3 is slower than JS (6.865s, +19%).
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten 3.1.18 with -O3 and -msimd128 (hand-written SIMD intrinsics in mul_mats_intrin.c); GCC 12.2.0 for the native rows (-O3, -O3 -mavx2); Node.js v16.16.0
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i5-1135G7 @ 2.40GHz, 16 GB RAM, Manjaro Linux kernel 5.19.1
tradeoffs: Needs the WebAssembly SIMD proposal (browser or Node support) and an Emscripten toolchain. The win comes from -O3 plus SIMD, not from Wasm alone.
caveats: Single 64x64 matrix-multiply microbenchmark from a 2022 Node 16 / Emscripten 3.1.18 setup; later V8 releases may have narrowed the gap. Without -O3 the Wasm build is 19% slower than JS. The native GCC -O3 scalar row (0.401s) is also beaten by the SIMD Wasm row but the -mavx2 native row (0.119s) is faster than any Wasm row. Demo repo, not a library.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'written in AssemblyScript "times faster" than pure JavaScript implementation benchmark' (github.com result jeromewu/wasm-perf)

name: wasm-i128-div-bench (reciprocal 128-bit division for the Wasm wide-arithmetic proposal)
baseline: Rust u128/i128 division operators lowering to compiler-builtins __udivti3/__umodti3 (compiler-rt libcall) on wasm32
workload: criterion microbenchmarks of 128-bit unsigned/signed divide, remainder and divrem, including a loop-invariant-divisor case, native vs V8 (d8) vs wasmtime (Cranelift), reciprocal (Moeller-Granlund) path vs the builtin operators.
claimed_speedup: Loop-invariant divisor (reciprocal hoisted): V8 d8 29.67 us -> 18.24 us (-38.5%), wasmtime 52.51 us -> 13.97 us (-73.4%), native 134.44 us -> 9.73 us (-92.8%). Single divisions are NOT faster on Wasm: V8 udivrem128 18.27 ns builtin vs 24.38 ns reciprocal (+33.4%), wasmtime +0.2%.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98.0-nightly (61d7280f3 2026-06-06), release profile opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, wasm32 target features +bulk-memory,+multivalue,+reference-types,+wide-arithmetic, build-std; d8 15.1.52; wasmtime 45.0.1
tradeoffs: Requires the wide-arithmetic Wasm proposal (V8 nightly, wasmtime 45 or later) and Rust nightly with build-std. Repo has no LICENSE file, so the code is reference-only. The README also sketches proposed i64.recip128 / i64.divrem_recip128 instructions.
caveats: Mixed result by design: the reciprocal path wins only when the divisor is loop-invariant and the reciprocal can be hoisted; for one-off divisions the builtin is faster or equal on V8 and wasmtime. Baseline is Rust's compiler-builtins, not TypeScript/JS or Emscripten C++. Single machine; the repo is a research micro-benchmark with no stars.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/MaxGraey?tab=repositories (AssemblyScript core developer's repo list, via the AssemblyScript built-with page)

name: eigen-js (Eigen C++ compiled to WebAssembly via Emscripten, in the mathjs benchmark suite)
baseline: mathjs (number-type and generic matrices); the same suite also runs sylvester, numeric.js and ndarray
workload: mathjs test/benchmark/matrix_operations.js (tinybench): A+A, A*A, A' (transpose) and det(A) on the benchmark's Fiedler matrix, eigen-js vs mathjs in Node.js.
claimed_speedup: eigen-js vs mathjs (number): A*A 5.31 us vs 29.24 us (about 5.5x, derived from page data); det(A) 3.96 us vs 218.70 us (about 55x, derived); A+A 2.21 us vs 5.14 us (about 2.3x, derived); transpose roughly equal (2.58 us vs 2.49 us).
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten (emcc) with embind, Eigen 3.3.9 subset, OSQP optional; flags not stated; benchmark run with tinybench (mathjs commit 7f02ba2)
tradeoffs: Manual memory management helper (garbage collector in the README); Wasm module load cost; only a subset of Eigen is exposed. It is a binding of Eigen (gitlab.com/libeigen/eigen is already catalogued), so the orchestrator may fold it as a duplicate/wrapper.
caveats: Run by the mathjs maintainer in a GitHub discussion (December 2024); machine, Node version and matrix size are not stated. The maintainer notes eigen-js is not an order of magnitude faster across the board: ndarray beats it on addition, transpose and determinant, and eigen-js ran out of memory under the default benchmark setup. The eigen-js README itself makes no performance claim.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'written in AssemblyScript "times faster" ... npm package WebAssembly' surfaced josdejong/mathjs discussion #2744 'Accelerated computations with WASM'

name: Pyodide (NumPy inv in WebAssembly vs math.js)
workload: Matrix inverse inv(rand(200,200)): numpy running in Pyodide (CPython and NumPy compiled to WebAssembly) in the browser vs math.js in Chrome and Safari, with native Python 3.10 numpy and Octave as references.
claimed_speedup: numpy in Pyodide 0.024 s vs math.js in Chrome 0.475 s (about 20x faster, derived from page data) and Safari 2.403 s; native numpy 0.009 s, Octave 0.005 s.
tradeoffs: Large download and startup cost for the Python runtime and NumPy (not measured in this comparison); results depend on browser Wasm engine.
caveats: Single timing posted by a third party (dvd101x, 2023-02-11) in a mathjs discussion; no machine, browser version or run count stated for the Pyodide row, and it is a single operation where NumPy calls compiled linear-algebra routines rather than interpreted Python. Load and warm-up time not included. The project itself publishes no such benchmark.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): josdejong/mathjs discussion #2744 (surfaced by WebSearch for AssemblyScript pure-JS speedup claims)

name: es-module-lexer (WebAssembly JS module lexer)
baseline: Acorn (the fastest pure-JS parser per the README) and the library's own CSP asm.js JavaScript build
workload: Parsing import/export syntax of JavaScript source: README parse times per MB on the 3.1 MB test/samples set via 'chomp bench', Wasm build vs asm.js/JS build; plus an Angular 1 (720KiB) parse vs Acorn.
claimed_speedup: Angular 1 (720KiB) fully parsed in 1ms vs over 100ms for Acorn. Wasm build 4.7 ms/MB cold and 3.2 ms/MB warm vs the JS (asm.js) build 14.9 ms/MB cold and 6.3 ms/MB warm (about 3.2x cold and 2.0x warm, derived from page data); minimal build 4.5 vs 10.8 ms/MB cold.
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten (upstream emsdk 6.0.0 for the Wasm builds, emsdk-fastcomp 1.40.1 for asm.js), built with Chomp; optimisation flags not stated; Node.js 26
tradeoffs: Only lexes import/export syntax, not a full parser; Wasm build 14.8KiB brotli; a pure-JS/asm.js build is provided for CSP environments and runtimes without Wasm.
caveats: First-party numbers without a stated CPU. The 'JS' comparison row is an asm.js compile of the same C source, not hand-written JavaScript. The Acorn comparison is one sentence with no methodology and Acorn does a full parse. Wasm is built by Emscripten from src/lexer.c, so this is C-via-Emscripten beating JS rather than a wasm-first language.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): README table in guybedford/es-module-lexer reached while checking wasm npm libraries for README benchmark tables

name: utf-as (UTF-8/UTF-16 transcoding and validation for AssemblyScript)
workload: UTF-8 encode and decode (and validation) over 15 HTML payloads taken from simdutf's benchmark fixtures, utf-as SIMD/SWAR kernels vs the AssemblyScript stdlib, run on V8.
claimed_speedup: UTF8.decode 2.1-6.7x faster than String.UTF8.decode; UTF8.encode 4.3-9.4x faster than String.UTF8.encode; UTF8.validate up to 55.4 GB/s on ASCII-heavy HTML (11.9-34.4 GB/s on other HTML); UTF16.validate up to 87 GB/s on surrogate-free HTML.
compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript with --enable simd (and recommended --enable bulk-memory); throughput figures measured with SIMD enabled on V8; SWAR path runs without SIMD
tradeoffs: Ports simdutf's Westmere SSE4 UTF-8 kernels to 128-bit Wasm SIMD. Drop-in signature parity with String.UTF8/UTF16; falls back to portable SWAR when SIMD is off, then only small-input gains. Decode is described as permissive rather than strict.
caveats: Baseline is AssemblyScript's own stdlib transcoder, not JavaScript TextEncoder/TextDecoder or a C++/Emscripten build. Headline numbers are in the README text and PNG charts; no CPU model is stated. Benchmark scripts (npm run bench:vs-stdlib, bench:simdutf) are in the repo so it is reproducible by a verifier. Very new, 1 star.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): AssemblyScript website 'Built with AssemblyScript' page (AssemblyScript/website src/built-with-assemblyscript.md) listing utf-as as 'Wickedly fast'

name: galois (finite-field arithmetic with AssemblyScript WebAssembly acceleration)
baseline: JavaScript BigInt arithmetic (256-bit and 128-bit prime fields) in the same library on Node.js
workload: Prime-field operations for modulus 2^128-k: additions, multiplications and exponentiations per second, JS BigInt vs the WASM implementation; README also says vector, matrix and polynomial operations speed up 6x-10x.
claimed_speedup: Additions 44,000,000 ops/s (WASM 128-bit) vs 5,000,000 (JS BigInt 128-bit) vs 3,200,000 (256-bit); multiplications 16,300,000 vs 1,850,000 vs 950,000; exponentiations 97,000 vs 10,500 vs 3,200 (about 8.8x, 8.8x and 9.2x vs 128-bit BigInt, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript 0.8.x (devDependency, loaded with @assemblyscript/loader); flags and Node.js version not stated
tradeoffs: WASM path exists only for prime fields with modulus 2^128-k (k < 2^64). README notes WASM memory cannot be freed, so FiniteField objects may need re-creation to avoid leaks.
caveats: The README calls these 'very informal benchmarks'; benchmark code is not linked from the README. Compared against JS BigInt, not against C++ or other WASM toolchains. Uses an old AssemblyScript 0.8 compiler and the last commit is from 2022.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): AssemblyScript website 'Built with AssemblyScript' page (Other Libraries: galois), then the README Performance section

name: cry-wasm (Ruby methods compiled to WebAssembly through Crystal)
baseline: CRuby (pure Ruby interpreter) running the same function
workload: Recursive Fibonacci fib(40) from examples/fib_bench.rb: pure Ruby vs the Crystal-compiled Wasm module called from Ruby via wasmtime-rb or wasmer-ruby.
claimed_speedup: ruby fib(40) 5.305503 s vs wasmtime 0.462232 s vs wasmer 0.381384 s (user time); README says 10x faster than Ruby, about 10% faster on Wasmer than Wasmtime (Dec 2022), and Wasm only about twice as slow as native by the author's measurements.
compiler_and_flags: Crystal compiler plus wasm-ld; Ripper and Sorcerer extract the Ruby source; flags not stated
tradeoffs: Needs type annotations on Ruby methods and the Crystal toolchain. Returning arrays from Wasm to Ruby is slow and can be slower than pure Ruby (README). Wasmer and Wasmtime first call is slower.
caveats: One recursive microbenchmark with no CPU model, from December 2022; the latest commit is only a dependency/CI bump, feature work dates from 2022. Baseline is CRuby, not the category's TypeScript/V8 or Emscripten baselines; shown here because Crystal-to-Wasm is a wasm-targeting route.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): awesome-wasm-langs README (appcypher) language list, then the cry-wasm README Benchmark section

name: xoroshiro128starstar (AssemblyScript WebAssembly seeded PRNG)
baseline: Math.random (V8) and the seedrandom npm package
workload: Generating random integers 0 <= n < 10, 'wasmrandom' vs Math.random vs seedrandom, via do-you-even-bench in Node.js.
claimed_speedup: wasmrandom 81,321,598.18 op/s vs Math.random 73,658,101.35 op/s (about 1.10x, derived from page data) vs seedrandom 24,057,933.98 op/s (about 3.4x, derived); the 262-byte module keeps its state in two u64 globals.
compiler_and_flags: asc -O3 (AssemblyScript from GitHub master, 2018) ; Node.js v10.3.0
tradeoffs: Small 262-byte module with no memory pages; seeded and reproducible unlike Math.random. Includes the JS/Wasm call overhead per number.
caveats: Node 10.3 era numbers, no CPU stated; the margin over Math.random is only about 10%, and the seeded JS competitor is seedrandom (a slower algorithm). Abandoned since 2019.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): AssemblyScript website 'Built with AssemblyScript' page (Crypto non-blockchain: xoroshiro128starstar), then the README Benchmark section

name: superfasthash (SuperFastHash in JavaScript and AssemblyScript WebAssembly)
baseline: JavaScript implementation of SuperFastHash in the same module (and Node.js native crypto MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, RIPEMD-160)
workload: 1,000,000 hashes timed by benchmarks/benchmark.js; the README shows the output as a screenshot (benchmark.png).
claimed_speedup: SuperFastHash (wasm) 369.101 ms vs SuperFastHash (js) 447.736 ms per 1,000,000 hashes (about 1.21x, derived from page data); native Node crypto: MD5 4437.191 ms, SHA-1 4436.841 ms, SHA-256 5154.750 ms, RIPEMD-160 6644.826 ms.
tradeoffs: Non-cryptographic hash only; Wasm path needs an async initialize() call.
caveats: Numbers exist only in a terminal screenshot in the repo; no CPU, Node version or compiler flags stated. The gain over JS is about 20% and includes JS-to-Wasm call overhead. The comparison with native crypto hashes is not like for like. Listed as unmaintained on awesome-assemblyscript.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): AssemblyScript website 'Built with AssemblyScript' page (Crypto non-blockchain: superfasthash); benchmark.png read from the repo

name: long.js (64-bit integer library with a WebAssembly fast path)
baseline: the library's own floating-point-based JavaScript fallback for 64-bit multiply, divide and remainder
workload: 64-bit integer multiplication, division and remainder through a tiny hand-written WebAssembly module (wasm.wat) vs the JavaScript fallback.
claimed_speedup: README: slow operations like division are 'around twice as fast' with the WebAssembly module.
tradeoffs: Falls back to the JS implementation where WebAssembly is unavailable; module is hand-written WAT, not a compiled language.
caveats: A one-line claim with no benchmark code, hardware or version in the README; baseline is the library's own JS fallback, not C++ or Emscripten. Included because the Wasm kernel is a long-lived, widely used example of a wasm path beating JS.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): README 'WebAssembly support' section of dcodeIO/long.js (AssemblyScript author's library), checked while surveying wasm libraries with speed claims
